![]({{plot}})

Which of the following statements are true with respect to the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is plotted above. 

- ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{-}}f(x)$ is finite
- ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{+}}f(x)$ is finite
- $f(x)$  has a discontinuity at $x={{a}}$
texts.:question/worked-solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is false. We get ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty .$

- Statement II is true. We get ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{+}}f(x)=3.$

- Statement III is true. The function contains a break exactly at $x={{a}}$ and it's impossible to draw its graph without taking our pencil off of the paper.

texts.:question/problem:
![]({{plot}})

Which of the following statements are true with respect to the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is plotted above. 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x={{a}}$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a}}}f(x)\ne f({{a}})$
- $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x={{a}}$
texts.:question/worked-solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. We have $f({{a}})=2.$

- Statement II is false. Indeed, from the graph we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{+}}f(x) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a}}}f(x)=2=f({{a}}).$

- Statement III is false. The graph of the function doesn't have a break at $x={{a}}$ and we can draw the graph of $f(x)$ around $x={{a}}$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is **not** defined at $x={{a}}$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a}}}f(x)$ exists
- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x={{a}}$
texts.:question/worked-solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. From the graph we can see that no value has been assigned to $f(x)$ at $x={{a}}.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{-}}f(x) & =3, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{+}}f(x) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 
${lim}_{x\to \,{{a}}}f(x)=3.$

- Statement III is false. The function is not even defined at $x={{a}}.$ The graph contains a break at $x={{a}}.$ It's impossible to draw the graph of $f(x)$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

![]({{plot}})

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x={{a}}$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a}}}f(x)$ exists
- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x={{a}}$
texts.:question/worked-solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. The function $f(x)$ is defined at $x={{a}}$ and we have $f({{a}})=1.$

- Statement II is false. We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{{a_power}}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, both left-hand side and right-hand side limits exist but they are not the same. Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,{{a}}}f(x)$ does not exist.

- Statement III is false. The function contains a break exactly at $x={{a}}$ and it's impossible to draw its graph without taking our pencil off of the paper.
